tour.title: Jewish Panama City: Communities, Archives and Memory
tour.subtitle: Five stops connecting Caribbean, European and Middle Eastern Jewish histories
tour.overview: A driving route linking Kol Shearith Israel and its museum, the Ashkenazi Beth El and Sephardi Shevet Ahim congregations, and Panama's public memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto fighters.
tour.mediaNote: Correct institutional reference images are recorded, but written reuse permission must be obtained before public publication because no suitable open-licence photographs were located during research.

stops.title: Kol Shearith Israel Synagogue
stops.address: Avenida de la Rotonda 18, Costa del Este, Panama City, Panama
stops.shortDescription: A Progressive congregation founded in 1876 by Sephardic families with roots in the Caribbean.
stops.fullDescription: Kol Shearith Israel was founded by families arriving largely from Curaçao, St Thomas and other Caribbean communities. Its Costa del Este centre, consecrated in 2006, contains synagogues, classrooms, archives and communal facilities. Visits must be arranged through the congregation and are subject to security.
stops.transcript: Kol Shearith Israel was founded in 1876, when Jewish families with strong connections to Curaçao, St Thomas and other Caribbean communities organised a congregation in Panama. Their history places Panama within a Sephardic Atlantic network shaped by trade, migration and family ties. The congregation later adopted Progressive Judaism and became a distinctive voice alongside the city's Orthodox communities. Its present Costa del Este centre was consecrated in 2006 and includes a main sanctuary, a smaller prayer space, classrooms, library, museum and gathering halls. That range of facilities shows how a synagogue can function as an entire communal campus. Panama's Jewish population is diverse, so this stop should not be presented as the city's single representative institution. Contact the congregation in advance, carry required identification and respect security instructions. The site introduces a theme repeated throughout the route: relatively small groups created durable institutions that connected religious tradition with participation in Panamanian national life.

stops.title: Panamanian Jewish Museum and Archives
stops.address: Avenida de la Rotonda 18, Costa del Este, Panama City, Panama
stops.shortDescription: A collection of family trees, cemetery and marriage records, oral histories and ritual objects within the KSI centre.
stops.fullDescription: The museum and Woodrow de Castro Library document the families who established Kol Shearith Israel and the wider Sephardic Caribbean context. Holdings include cemetery records from 1876, marriage records from 1885, biographies, family trees, religious objects and the Jewish Oral History Project of Panama. Access requires prior arrangement.
stops.transcript: Inside the Kol Shearith Israel centre, the Panamanian Jewish Museum and Jewish Archives preserve the evidence from which community history can be written. Family trees show connections across Caribbean ports; marriage certificates and cemetery records turn broad migration patterns into named lives. The collection includes religious objects, books, biographies and oral histories recorded with Panamanian Jews. These sources are especially valuable because everyday community experience does not always appear in national archives or monumental architecture. The Woodrow de Castro Library places Panama within the wider history of Sephardic Jews in the Caribbean and the Americas. This stop shares the synagogue's location but has a separate purpose: it asks how records, memory and family stewardship create a usable past. Access is not guaranteed and must be arranged with the congregation. Researchers and visitors should respect privacy restrictions, particularly for recent family material. A museum of this scale demonstrates that preservation can begin within a community long before its history is widely known outside it.

stops.title: Beth El Synagogue
stops.address: Calle Winston Churchill, Punta Paitilla, Panama City, Panama
stops.shortDescription: The principal institution of Panama City's Ashkenazi Orthodox community, founded by Central European arrivals around the Second World War.
stops.fullDescription: Beth El developed from an Ashkenazi community established by immigrants and refugees from Europe in the 1940s. The modern Paitilla centre supports worship, education and family life for a community now shaped by migration from across the Americas as well as Panama-born generations. Visits require advance approval.
stops.transcript: Beth El tells the Ashkenazi chapter of Panama City's Jewish history. The community was organised in the 1940s by families who had arrived from Central Europe around the Second World War. Early members met in homes before acquiring communal premises, building religious and social structures for people separated from the places where their customs had developed. Over time the congregation expanded, and the modern Paitilla centre created space for prayer, study, children and community events. More recent members have come from Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina, Uruguay, North America and elsewhere, making Ashkenazi life here both rooted and continually renewed. This is an Orthodox synagogue, but individual members represent varied levels of observance. It is a private, secure community rather than a walk-in tourist attraction. Arrange any visit in advance, dress modestly and follow instructions. Compare Beth El with Kol Shearith Israel: the differences are not merely labels but histories of migration, ritual and organisation coexisting within one city.

stops.title: Shevet Ahim Synagogue
stops.address: Calle 43 Este, Bella Vista, Panama City, Panama
stops.shortDescription: The central synagogue of Panama's large Sephardic community, shaped especially by families from Syria and Lebanon.
stops.fullDescription: Founded in 1933, Shevet Ahim became a major institution for Jews arriving from Syria and Lebanon. Its Orthodox Sephardic worship, schools, welfare and kosher infrastructure helped create a closely connected community with a strong place in Panamanian commerce and civic life. Security and religious practice require coordinated access.
stops.transcript: Shevet Ahim was founded in 1933 as growing numbers of Jewish families from Syria and Lebanon made Panama their home. They brought Sephardic and Middle Eastern liturgical traditions, family networks and communal structures that differed from both the Caribbean-rooted KSI congregation and the Ashkenazi Beth El community. Shevet Ahim developed into a major centre of daily prayer, Torah study, education, welfare and family celebrations. Its importance helps explain why Jewish infrastructure in Panama City is unusually extensive for the country's size. Yet community strength should not be reduced to commercial stereotypes; religious practice, charitable responsibility and intergenerational life are equally important. The synagogue is active and security-sensitive. Visitors must make arrangements rather than appear unannounced, and should observe modest dress and Shabbat restrictions. This stop makes the plural structure of Jewish Panama visible: several congregations preserve distinct customs while participating in a shared national community.

stops.title: Warsaw Ghetto Fighters Monument
stops.address: Calle José Isaac Fábrega near Colegio La Salle, Panama City, Panama
stops.shortDescription: A public monument connecting Panama with the memory of Jewish resistance during the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.
stops.fullDescription: The monument honours those who resisted German forces during the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Its placement in Panama City shows how Holocaust remembrance entered public landscapes far beyond Europe and Israel. The GPS point is decoded from the published full location code and should receive an on-site verification before production release.
stops.transcript: This public monument links Panama City to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of April and May 1943. Jewish fighters, facing deportation and almost certain death, resisted German forces sent to liquidate the ghetto. Their struggle became a global symbol of Jewish resistance, although remembrance must also include the civilians who hid, cared for others and endured the destruction around them. A monument in Panama reflects the international movement to commemorate the uprising and the personal connections of local Jewish families to European catastrophe. It also moves Holocaust memory beyond the walls of a synagogue or museum into shared civic space. Examine the inscription and figures carefully, and distinguish the 1943 Jewish uprising from the wider Warsaw Uprising of 1944. The location is outdoors and publicly accessible. Before production publication, the precise marker position should be confirmed on site because current map databases identify the monument through a location code rather than a surveyed OpenStreetMap feature.
